query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, continuous hexagonal boron-nitride (h-BN) surface coating to dense TiB₂ ceramic parts used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment will cut their molten-aluminum corrosion rate by at least a factor of five relative to uncoated TiB₂ under standard bath conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Fully dense (>97% theoretical) polycrystalline TiB₂ coupons (10 mm × 10 mm × 3 mm) produced by hot pressing; as-polished surface roughness Ra ≤ 0.2 µm.
generation.intervention: Chemical-vapour deposition of a 2 ± 0.5 µm adherent h-BN layer on all exposed surfaces.
generation.conditions: Static bath of 99.5 wt % molten Al at 750 ± 5 °C for 24 h in argon cover gas; no deliberate flux additions; samples fully immersed; flow <0.05 m s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: Dense, crystalline h-BN barrier layer that remains chemically inert and poorly wetted by Al, supplemented by a thin AlN/Al₂O₃ interlayer that forms in-situ and further impedes aluminum ingress.
generation.mechanism:
1) h-BN has extremely low solubility in, and low interfacial energy with, molten aluminum, so it is not readily dissolved or wetted.
2) The coating blocks direct contact between Al(l) and TiB₂, preventing formation of Ti-Al intermetallics or AlB₂ that normally drive dissolution.
3) Any dissolved nitrogen/oxygen promotes a nanometric AlN–Al₂O₃ complex film at the interface, increasing chemical resistance and adhesion of the BN layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Mean mass-loss rate will be ≤0.2 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹ (≥80 % lower than the ~1 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹ typical for uncoated TiB₂ under the same conditions). Cross-sectional SEM/EDS will show ≤3 µm reaction layer on coated parts vs >15 µm on controls.
generation.baseline: Uncoated TiB₂ coupons subjected to the identical molten-Al exposure.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is expected up to 900 °C, provided the BN layer remains continuous (>95 % area coverage) and mechanically undamaged; aggressive fluxing salts or strong bath agitation may disrupt the coating and nullify the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate: Direct quantitative data for CVD-BN on TiB₂ in molten Al are sparse; prediction extrapolates from BN wettability studies on graphite and TiB₂ in Al alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups (n = 5 each) of TiB₂ coupons: Group A uncoated, Group B coated with 2 µm CVD-BN. Characterize coating thickness/uniformity (SEM, XPS). Immerse both groups simultaneously in a graphite-lined crucible containing 99.5 % Al at 750 °C for 24 h under argon. After quench, remove adherent aluminum mechanically, ultrasonically clean, and measure mass change. Cross-section and image by SEM/EDS to measure reaction-layer thickness and identify phases.
measurements: Mass loss per unit area (mg cm⁻² h⁻¹)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the average mass-loss rate reduction of Group B relative to Group A is <20 % OR if ≥3 of 5 coated samples exhibit continuous reaction layers >10 µm thick, indicating loss of barrier function.
